transcript.content:
I've been looking forward to this all week -- it would absolutely make my day if the Moon happened to be visible right now.

I'm in La Paz, Bolivia at 2026-11-11 12:27 -04 (UTC-0400) (2026-11-11T16:27:00Z in UTC), at latitude -16.4897 degrees and longitude -68.1193 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 87.281 degrees and its azimuth is 246.697 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 64.177 degrees and its azimuth is 119.602 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 5.54 percent illuminated, 27.157 degrees from the Sun, and 397875.5 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest with you: **No, it is extremely unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes under these specific conditions.**

While your app correctly shows that the Moon is "above the horizon," there are three major factors working against you right now:

### 1. The "Washout" Effect (Sun's Altitude)
The Sun is currently at an altitude of **87.281 degrees**. This means it is nearly at its zenith (directly overhead). At this angle, the atmosphere is scattering a massive amount of sunlight. Even though the Moon is technically "up," the sheer volume of scattered light in the sky creates a "white-out" effect. It is very similar to trying to see a lightbulb turned on in a room where the overhead floodlights are at full blast.

### 2. The Moon's Phase (Illumination)
The Moon is only **5.54% illuminated**. This means you are looking at a very thin crescent. Because the Moon is only 27 degrees away from the Sun, it is physically positioned in the brightest part of the sky. The "daylight" is so intense that the faint reflection of the Sun off that tiny sliver of the Moon won't provide enough contrast to be visible against the blue of the sky.

### 3. Atmospheric Scattering
Because you are in La Paz (which has a high altitude, which helps!), the air is thinner, but the sun is still incredibly powerful. At 12:27 PM, the blue light scattering (Rayleigh scattering) is at its peak. To see the Moon during the day, you usually need it to be much further from the Sun (a "Daytime Moon" that is more than 40–50 degrees away) or for the Moon to be much fuller.

### The Verdict
If you look toward the azimuth of **119.6 degrees** (which is roughly East-Southeast), you will see a very bright, washed-out sky. You might see a slight "haze" or a subtle change in the texture of the blue sky where the Moon is located, but your eyes will not be able to resolve the distinct shape of the lunar disk.

**The good news:** Since the Moon is moving, it will continue to move further away from the Sun as the day progresses. If you wait until later this evening when the Sun has set and the ambient light has dropped, the Moon will be much easier to spot!
